```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(survey) # Required for complex survey variance estimation
```

## 1. Introduction
This report investigates the utilization, unit economics, and safety profile of GLP-1 receptor agonists (Semaglutide). Initially, we hypothesized that financial incentives drove off-label cosmetic use, resulting in a disproportionate rise in inappropriate use and harm.

However, through rigorous ontological separation of MedDRA adverse event terms and canonical case deduplication, we demonstrate that the initial safety signal was an artifact of definitional circularity.

```{r load_data}
cms_data <- read_csv("../data/processed/cms_volume_output.csv")
faers_data <- read_csv("../data/processed/faers_full_ml_data.csv")
meps_data <- read_csv("../data/processed/meps_financial_output.csv")
```

## 2. The Result: Medicare Part D Volume
Medicare Part D statutorily excludes weight-loss indications, so CMS volume reflects primarily diabetes use. Nonetheless, Semaglutide shows massive growth.

```{r volume_growth, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
ggplot(cms_data, aes(x = year, y = total_prescriptions / 1e6, color = generic_name, group = generic_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(
    title = "Prescription Volume Trends (2020-2024)",
    subtitle = "Medicare Part D Total Claims (Primarily Diabetes Use)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Total Prescriptions (Millions)",
    color = "Drug Cohort"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## 3. The Motive: Unit Economics (Survey-Weighted)
Using the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), we calculate the true national average cost per prescription. Because MEPS is a stratified cluster sample, we utilize the `survey` package with `VARSTR` and `VARPSU` to calculate design-based standard errors and 95% Confidence Intervals.

```{r financial_motive, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
# Filter to 2024 (or latest available year in your subset)
meps_latest <- meps_data %>% filter(year == max(year))

# Build the complex survey design object on the FULL dataset
meps_design <- svydesign(
  id = ~varpsu,
  strata = ~varstr,
  weights = ~weight,
  data = meps_latest,
  nest = TRUE
)

# Subset to only our target/control drugs to preserve survey variance
meps_sub_design <- subset(meps_design, generic_name != 'OTHER')

# Calculate survey-weighted means and standard errors
cost_estimates <- svyby(~spending, ~generic_name, meps_sub_design, svymean)

ggplot(cost_estimates, aes(x = reorder(generic_name, spending), y = spending, fill = generic_name)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper), width = 0.2, size = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("$", round(spending, 0))), hjust = -0.5, size = 5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(
    title = "Unit Economics Comparison",
    subtitle = "Average Cost per Prescription (MEPS Weighted National Estimates with 95% CIs)",
    x = "",
    y = "Average Cost per Prescription ($)",
    fill = "Drug Cohort"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## 4. Pharmacovigilance: Resolving Definitional Circularity
A naive analysis grouping "Off-label use" with "Medication Errors" yields a massive risk increase for the Weight Loss cohort. However, "Off-label use" is definitionally circular with prescribing Ozempic for weight loss.

When we restrict the outcome strictly to operational harm (Medication Errors, Counterfeits, Overdoses), the signal flips. The Weight Loss cohort actually reports *fewer* medication errors than the Diabetes cohort.

```{r off_label_signal, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
# Calculate the percentage of cases involving actual medication errors
misuse_summary <- faers_data %>%
  filter(indication %in% c("Weight Loss", "Diabetes")) %>%
  group_by(drug, indication) %>%
  summarise(
    total_cases = sum(total_cases),
    med_error_cases = sum(med_error_cases),
    pct_error = (med_error_cases / total_cases) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(cohort = paste(drug, "(", indication, ")"))

ggplot(misuse_summary, aes(x = reorder(cohort, pct_error), y = pct_error, fill = indication)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct_error, 1), "%")), hjust = -0.2, size = 5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(
    title = "True Medication Error & Counterfeit Signals",
    subtitle = "Percentage of total cases reporting operational harm (excluding definitional off-label use)",
    x = "",
    y = "Percentage of Total Cases (%)",
    fill = "Indication"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, max(misuse_summary$pct_error, na.rm=TRUE) * 1.2))
```

## 5. Limitations & Scientific Conclusions
FAERS is a spontaneous reporting system and cannot estimate incidence. Our Inferential Grouped-Binomial GLM revealed that consumers are vastly more likely to report these events than healthcare professionals, indicating a strong "Weber effect" (media-stimulated reporting).

Furthermore, MEPS provides gross expenditure per fill, not manufacturer margin, and CMS Part D suppresses small prescriber-drug cells. Therefore, while the financial incentives (unit economics) are astronomically high, the available data cannot establish a causal chain that this drove marketing which resulted in harm. In fact, after canonical case deduplication and strict MedDRA ontological boundaries, the data suggests the cosmetic weight-loss cohort is at a *lower* risk for medication errors than the standard diabetes cohort.
